lessons.title: What Australian music is, and who decides
lessons.contentPoint: Identity, values and experience in a work
lessons.intention: We are learning how music reflects the identity and experience of the people who make it.
criteria: I can explain what a work reflects about the people who made it.
steps: The question opened rather than answered: is a work Australian because of where it was made, who made it, what it is about, or how it sounds?
Three contrasting works from the register examined for the identities and experiences they reflect.
Students write a provisional answer and keep it to revisit in Week 10.
resources: Listening set from the repertoire register.
lessons.enduring: A work reflects personal and shared identities, values and experiences.

lessons.title: The well-formed dot point, taught explicitly
lessons.contentPoint: Terminology and text structures
lessons.intention: We are learning to write an analytical dot point in the form a marker expects.
criteria: I can write a dot point with a feature, a location and a reason.
steps: The dot point taught as a form: the feature, what it sounds like and where in the excerpt, then why it is there.
Text structure and terminology taught together, because a precise word in the wrong structure still loses the mark.
Three dot points written on one short excerpt and marked live.
lessons.enduring: Music applies ALARM to build well-formed dot points, not paragraphs.

lessons.title: Aural routine in examination format
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in repertoire
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse the elements of music under examination conditions.
criteria: I can write an analytical response to a single element in the time allowed.
steps: The weekly aural routine moves into examination format from this week: excerpt played three times, one element, written response.
The timing of the real paper introduced now so it is routine by Week 8.
Responses marked against the AT3 criteria and returned the same lesson.
lessons.enduring: An examination measures a routine that was built long before the paper.

lessons.title: One element per dot point: pitch and melody
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in repertoire
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse pitch and melody precisely.
criteria: I can describe a melody's shape and range and say what it achieves.
steps: Pitch and melody in Australian repertoire: range, contour, intervals and where the melody sits in the texture.
The same excerpt heard three times with a different pitch question each time.
Timed writing: two dot points on melody, marked against the criteria.
lessons.enduring: Precision about one element beats vagueness about four.

lessons.title: Identity in a song: whose experience is this
lessons.contentPoint: Identity, values and experience in a work
lessons.intention: We are learning to explain how a work reflects shared understandings and values.
criteria: I can point to a musical feature that carries the meaning of a work.
steps: A work examined for whose experience it carries and how the music carries it, not only the lyric.
Values and identity in music discussed with care and with evidence.
Written response: one dot point on a musical feature that carries the meaning.
lessons.enduring: The meaning of a work is carried by the music, not only by the words.

lessons.title: Playing an Australian work
lessons.contentPoint: Interpreting a range of genres and styles
lessons.intention: We are learning to interpret repertoire from a particular genre and style.
criteria: I can play in the style of the work rather than just the notes of it.
steps: The class band plays an Australian work from the register, interpreting rather than reproducing it.
The genre's conventions identified in the playing: what has to be right for this to sound like what it is.
Performance recorded for comparison with the original.
lessons.enduring: Performing a style is applying its conventions, not only its pitches.

lessons.title: One element per dot point: texture and tone colour
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in repertoire
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse texture and tone colour precisely.
criteria: I can describe the layers in an excerpt and what each contributes.
steps: Texture and tone colour analysed in three Australian works: how many layers, what each is doing, and what each sound source contributes.
Layer-by-layer listening with the mix isolated where recordings allow.
Timed writing: two dot points, marked against the criteria.
lessons.enduring: Texture is countable, and counting it is where the analysis starts.

lessons.title: Structure and duration in the same excerpt
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in repertoire
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse structure and duration as separate questions.
criteria: I can map an excerpt's structure and describe its use of duration.
steps: Structure and duration: sections, proportions, metre, tempo and how the piece uses time.
One excerpt mapped for structure, then the same excerpt analysed for duration, so students feel the difference between the two questions.
Timed writing under examination conditions.
lessons.enduring: Two questions about time are not the same question.

lessons.title: Marking a dot point against the criteria
lessons.contentPoint: Terminology and text structures
lessons.intention: We are learning to judge a response the way a marker judges it.
criteria: I can award a mark against the criteria and justify it.
steps: Students mark real responses, anonymised, against the AT3 marking criteria, then justify the marks awarded.
The marker's view made visible: what a vague response costs and why.
Each student remarks their own Week 1 response.
lessons.enduring: Understanding the criteria is faster than guessing what is wanted.

lessons.title: AT3 issued: what the paper examines
lessons.contentPoint: Terminology and text structures
lessons.intention: We are learning what AT3 asks for and how the term's work prepares for it.
criteria: I can describe the paper's structure and what each part asks of me.
steps: Assessment Task 3 issued: an aural paper of about 30 minutes, sat in Week 8. It names the elements it examines.
The shape of the paper: objective identification items, short written answers, one partly unseen excerpt, no extended response.
Students map the paper against the writing they have already done.
lessons.enduring: Nothing on the paper is a surprise except the excerpt.

lessons.title: Protocols first
lessons.contentPoint: Place, Country and Languages, and protocols
lessons.intention: We are learning the protocols that govern how we study this music.
criteria: I can state the protocols that apply and why they exist.
steps: Before any listening: the protocols for studying the music of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.
What the class may do with this material, what it may not do, and why permission and attribution are not formalities.
The school's consultation process explained, including that repertoire for this block is chosen through it.
lessons.enduring: Protocols come before the listening, not alongside it.

lessons.title: Place, Country and Languages in the music
lessons.contentPoint: Place, Country and Languages, and protocols
lessons.intention: We are learning to identify and describe how Place, Country and Languages are reflected in this music.
criteria: I can describe how a work reflects Place, Country or Languages.
steps: How Place, Country and Languages are reflected in the music, heard in repertoire selected through consultation.
The relationship between a work and the Country it belongs to, described in the terms the community uses.
Written response with the protocols applied to the way it is written.
lessons.enduring: Understanding the protocols informs how the music is studied and interpreted.

lessons.title: Listening with the protocols applied
lessons.contentPoint: Place, Country and Languages, and protocols
lessons.intention: We are learning to apply respectful protocols while we analyse.
criteria: I can analyse this music and attribute it correctly.
steps: Extended listening from the consulted repertoire, with the protocols explicitly applied to how the class listens, discusses and writes.
Attribution practised: naming the artist, the community and the source correctly, every time.
Timed writing on one element.
lessons.enduring: Correct attribution is part of the analysis, not an afterthought.

lessons.title: How music influences and challenges ideas
lessons.contentPoint: Music influencing and challenging ideas
lessons.intention: We are learning how music can influence and challenge ideas.
criteria: I can explain what a work argued and how the music carried the argument.
steps: Music as an argument: how a work can influence and challenge ideas at local, national and international levels.
One Australian work examined for what changed because of it.
Written response: two dot points, one on a musical feature and one on its effect.
lessons.enduring: Music does work in the world, and the working is audible.

lessons.title: Music and public argument in Australia
lessons.contentPoint: Music influencing and challenging ideas
lessons.intention: We are learning to evaluate music's effect at more than one scale.
criteria: I can distinguish a local effect from a national one and give evidence.
steps: A second work examined for the same question in a different decade, so the point is about music rather than about one song.
Cultural understanding developed at local, national and international levels, named as three different scales of effect.
Timed writing under examination conditions.
lessons.enduring: The same music can mean different things at different distances.

lessons.title: Performing music created or inspired by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
lessons.contentPoint: Cultural significance and protocols in performance
lessons.intention: We are learning to apply protocols when performing this music.
criteria: I can state what I must check before performing this work and do it.
steps: Performance of repertoire selected through the school's consultation, with the protocols applied to the performance itself.
What may be performed, by whom, in what setting, and what must be asked first.
Rehearsal with attribution stated as part of the performance.
lessons.enduring: Cultural significance and protocols apply to performing, not only to listening.

lessons.title: Cultural significance in performance
lessons.contentPoint: Cultural significance and protocols in performance
lessons.intention: We are learning that cultural significance changes how music should be performed.
criteria: I can explain how the significance of this work affects the way we play it.
steps: The performance refined, with attention to what the music is for and how that changes how it should be played.
Discussion of restrictions and permissions as musical facts rather than administrative ones.
Recorded, with the recording's use agreed in advance.
lessons.enduring: How a work is performed is part of respecting what it is.

lessons.title: Australian art music
lessons.contentPoint: Analysing elements in repertoire
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse the elements of music in Australian art music.
criteria: I can analyse an art music work using the correct terminology.
steps: Australian art music studied as the unit's art music thread: the notated concert tradition here, and composers writing in and against it.
One work analysed across two elements, with the terminology of the concert tradition taught alongside.
Timed writing, marked against the criteria.
resources: Art music listening set from the repertoire register.
lessons.enduring: The concert tradition is one Australian music among several.

lessons.title: The first cold excerpt
lessons.contentPoint: Evaluating how elements are manipulated and combined
lessons.intention: We are learning to analyse a work we have never heard before.
criteria: I can produce a full response to an unfamiliar excerpt in the time allowed.
steps: The first genuinely unseen excerpt, checked against the repertoire register so it is unseen in fact and not only in intention.
Method for an unfamiliar work: what to listen for first, second and third, and what to write while the excerpt is still playing.
Full timed response, marked and returned the same lesson.
resources: Unseen excerpt verified against the repertoire register.
lessons.enduring: An unseen excerpt tests listening, which is why it cannot be a work the class has met.

lessons.title: Writing the context sentence
lessons.contentPoint: Context written up with correct terminology
lessons.intention: We are learning to write about context in the form an examination expects.
criteria: I can write a context statement that is supported by what I heard.
steps: Context written in examination form: what the excerpt suggests about style, culture, history or society, in correct terminology and without invention.
The difference between a defensible inference and a guess, shown in marked examples.
Timed writing on context only.
lessons.enduring: A context claim has to be supported by the sound, not by a hunch.

lessons.title: Examination technique
lessons.contentPoint: Context written up with correct terminology
lessons.intention: We are learning the technique that makes the paper survivable.
criteria: I can budget my time across the paper and use each playing for a different purpose.
steps: Reading the question, budgeting the time, and using the three playings differently rather than identically.
What to do when the first playing produces nothing, and how to recover on the second.
Full practice paper begun under timing.
lessons.enduring: Technique is worth marks that knowledge alone does not collect.

lessons.title: Last practice paper, marked in class
lessons.contentPoint: Evaluating how elements are manipulated and combined
lessons.intention: We are learning to find and close our own gaps before the real paper.
criteria: I can identify my weakest question type and say how I will handle it.
steps: Final practice paper sat under full conditions, then marked in class against the guideline.
The two questions that cost the class the most marks identified and retaught on the spot.
Each student writes one line on what they will do differently on Thursday.
lessons.enduring: The last rehearsal is for finding the gap, not for confirming the strengths.

lessons.title: AT3 sat
lessons.contentPoint: Evaluating how elements are manipulated and combined
lessons.intention: We are learning to evaluate how the elements are manipulated and combined under examination conditions.
criteria: I can complete the paper in the time allowed, with a response to every question.
steps: Assessment Task 3 sat: aural paper, about 30 minutes, under examination conditions.
Objective identification items and short written answers, one partly unseen excerpt, no extended response.
Papers collected and the excerpt list confirmed against the register for the record.
resources: AT3 paper, audio and answer booklets.
lessons.enduring: The paper measures the routine, and the routine has been running since Week 1.

lessons.title: Post-paper debrief
lessons.contentPoint: Evaluating how elements are manipulated and combined
lessons.intention: We are learning from the paper while it is still fresh.
criteria: I can say which question type cost me marks and why.
steps: Immediate debrief while the paper is fresh: which excerpt was hardest and why, and what the class would want to have practised more.
The unseen excerpt replayed and analysed properly, without marks attached.
Notes taken for the Term 4 and Year 10 planning.
lessons.enduring: The debrief is worth more than the mark if it happens the same week.

lessons.title: Arranging an Australian work
lessons.contentPoint: Adapting or arranging for new purposes
lessons.intention: We are learning to arrange an existing work for a different purpose and audience.
criteria: I can plan an arrangement that suits the players in this room.
steps: An Australian work from the term's repertoire arranged for the people and instruments actually in the room.
What changes when the forces change: register, texture, who carries the melody and what is lost.
Arrangement plan drafted and logged.
lessons.enduring: Arranging is a decision about purpose, audience and forces.

lessons.title: Protocols when arranging
lessons.contentPoint: Cultural significance and protocols in composing
lessons.intention: We are learning to apply protocols when we adapt somebody else's music.
criteria: I can check my arrangement against the protocols and say what I may not change.
steps: Cultural significance and respectful protocols applied to arranging, including what may not be arranged and why.
Permission, attribution and intellectual property in a real case.
Each arrangement plan checked against the protocols before work continues.
lessons.enduring: Some material may be studied and not adapted, and knowing the difference is the skill.

lessons.title: Arrangement workshop, draft 1
lessons.contentPoint: Adapting or arranging for new purposes
lessons.intention: We are learning to test an arrangement by playing it.
criteria: I can identify what is not working in my arrangement once I hear it.
steps: First draft played in the room, badly, and fixed in front of the class.
The gap between the plan and the sound identified and closed.
Log entry on what changed when the arrangement was first heard.
lessons.enduring: An arrangement is a hypothesis until somebody plays it.

lessons.title: Arrangement workshop, draft 2
lessons.contentPoint: Adapting or arranging for new purposes
lessons.intention: We are learning to refine an arrangement through rehearsal.
criteria: I can bring my arrangement to a standard the class can perform.
steps: Second draft rehearsed, with the fixes from draft one applied.
Balance, entries and endings rehearsed as they were in Term 1.
Final parts printed and the running order set.
lessons.enduring: The second draft is where the arrangement becomes playable.

lessons.title: Arrangements performed to the class
lessons.contentPoint: Interpreting a range of genres and styles
lessons.intention: We are learning to interpret and present a work we have arranged.
criteria: I can present my arrangement and explain the decisions in it.
steps: Arrangements performed to the class, unmarked, with the attribution stated before each.
Each arranger says in one sentence what they changed and why.
Recorded for the process log and for the evidence file.
lessons.enduring: Presenting the reasoning is part of presenting the work.

lessons.title: AT3 feedback, and the log entry that closes the term
lessons.contentPoint: Context written up with correct terminology
lessons.intention: We are learning to use examination feedback to improve the next piece of writing.
criteria: I can rewrite a weak response and show what improved.
steps: Marked papers returned with written feedback, read against the criteria rather than against the mark.
Each student writes a context response again, on the excerpt they did worst on, and compares the two.
Term closed by naming what Term 4 needs: the writing turns into a rationale.
lessons.enduring: Feedback that does not produce a rewrite has not been used.
